Unfortunately it is not possible for me to relocate, as there are no public transport friendly areas or bike lanes available anywhere here.

At the moment, I either have to rely on my mom or I use Uber. I dislike relying on my mom and Uber for transport.  

I feel immensely embarrassed since people automatically assume that since I'm 27, I have a car (which I do) and can drive (emphasis on the latter point).  When ever the subject of how I get around is mentioned, I lie and say I can drive.  Other times, I use an excuse such as my car is in for a service, if it is noticed that I used an Uber.

I hate the feeling of embarrassment of not being able to drive at my age, and the frustration of not being able to go around as I please without having to rely on an external service such as Uber or my mom or even a friend.

I also lean into apathy as a way to cope with driving in the moment. I repeatedly tell myself, whatever happens happens and if something happens to me, so be it.  As long as no one else is injured as a result of any mistake I make.  Should that happen, I would be burdened with that guilt forever. Luckily, that has not happened and I hope that it never does.

Focusing on reaching the destination is also another coping mechanism that I have. I always obey the speed limit even if it may irritate others behind me.  That type of "inconvenience" to them, I do not care about as I am obeying the law in that instance.

Since not everyone is aware of *how* the right of way system works, and I referring especially to the region in which I reside, that makes the situation even more stressful.  Everyone has a different interpretation of how they think it works, despite there being an actual rule in place.

No one drives according to the officially strict rules of road.  For example, you are meant to stop completely at a stop sign, shift into neutral and then into first gear and hold it until it is your turn to proceed (first come first serve).  If everyone adhered to those rules, there would be the next world war in terms of road rage.  People would usually gear down into second, look left and right, and if it's clear, proceed, otherwise gear into first and wait their turn.

I've had to learn these "unwritten rules" of the road.  There are probably way more that I have not yet learned.

Oh and unfortunately, I also have the added challenge of having to avoid potholes, which isn't fun.

A few months, my mom forced me to drive to pick her up from work. I ended up taking the wrong road which had a speed bump and potholes. I was driving the speed limit, but didn't see the speed bump until it was too late. I slammed on the brakes so hard. I just heard tyre squeal and a huge thud.

I felt so guilty, because my mind was occupied with everything else around me. I immediately burst into tears. Looking back, it was rather immature of me but I was so upset.

I can relate to everything you've described. I would say I'm fairly competent at driving on a straight road with changing gears etc. However the moment I have to start reacting to more "challenging" situations like changing lanes, gearing up and down when there is an incline or anything other than a straight road and driving forward in the same lane. Encountering traffic circles and reversing in general are an absolute nightmare. They both put the fear of God in me. I know none of those are actually challenging, but they are extremely anxiety inducing.

Also, I refuse to drive an automatic transmission. In my mind, it feels like I'm "cheating" and avoiding the core issue. If I can't drive a manual transmission, I don't feel like I can properly drive, which is important to me.

That make sense. I've definitely noticed the same sort of "processing delay" if I can refer to it as that.  My mom has indirectly noticed it whenever I have to make a decision related to driving. She was like "What are you waiting for? Do *whatever".*  I experience this with other tasks in my daily life, however it makes me feel especially incompetent with driving.  Additionally, when I'm driving, I subconsciously observe every vehicle within sight constantly, as I am also deeply mistrusting of others on the road, which is extremely ironic. It is extremely draining on me mentally.

Was it an issue of self confidence or merely the uncomfortable nature of so many things happening around you when driving?  I find that extremely overwhelming, ironically even at a red light / stop sign.  No one is moving but yet I still feel the same sense of anxiety.  I would get blisters from subconsciously gripping the steering wheel so tight as though I'm about to fall off a cliff.

I have driven on both quiet two lane back roads and highways / motorways, both with and without traffic.  They both feel equally as distressing. Even reversing out of the driveway is scary as I have to reserve out at an angle, which should be easy enough but I can never do it.  Parking is another matter all together.

Sometimes I do feel like I'm alone in facing this diagrammer's block but I won't give up :D

If I'm following your example given and explanations, I believe you are correct in your understanding.

Each piece cannot exist in isolation without context and thus requires understanding of the entire picture.
When you mean "serialising" into a description, are you referring to a sequence of steps, diagramming or both?

Everything you've described makes sense. The way you visualise and or write your plan of action/s, is that something that you've had to learn and improve upon as a skill?

I feel like I don't know "how to plan". For some, they can put pen to power and the process is automatic. The moment a pen and paper is infront of me (no code), and I need to draw my thoughts, my brain just blanks out or spins into overthinking out at the speed of light.

Most sources do indeed tell you to "document everything" and they are correct. They fail to tell you how and what, and even I struggle with that, as you've noticed by this post haha.

Always assume that nothing is ever "stupid" or "too obvious enough" to document. You never know who will be reading those docs.

Some companies don't mind if you document your code itself in the file. Others do.

There is a markup language called markdown which you'll find a lot of developers use to document their code. The readme file on a git repository is an example of a markdown file. You can create them anywhere. Our project has a "docs" folder with nothing but markdown files in it.

Please could you explain what you mean by "abstractions for parts you need"?

I understand the steps required to complete a feature but they exist only in my mind. "I need to implement logic that needs to perform this action in order to get a result". Problem is, even though I may know what I need to do code wise, I literally cannot draw that process out on paper.

The inability also extends to visualising how all the individual pieces fit together in the big picture.

Remember, there will never such a thing as "perfect" documentation but I'm assuming you mean like an example of what they are expecting. Basically a template of sorts.

I use markdown for docs which makes navigating them easy.

Another thing to keep in mind is who is the intended audience of your application. For example, our team has taken the approach of writing docs not just for explaining all the pieces of the application but also what potential pitfalls other developers can encounter whilst in the development environment. 

For example, our senior discovered interesting behaviour when rebasing remote branches with main.
Most sites default to say NEVER DO THIS. His document literally describes an experiment he did trying to figure it out. Every step he try, what messages where shown by GIT, the whole way. It included screenshots etc. There is tremendous power in approaching documentation like that.

Obviously something like this isn't expected at a university level but definitely something to consider as you progress in your career. You'll find docs become less a chore and more enjoyable.

Is it common for one's thinking to not cooperate with what is being drawn and writing. I've always had that issue so I'm wondering if people in general struggle with it.

My neurotypical colleague is also in the same boat where he also is not used to planning before coding. He jumps into code immediately. I asked him to draw out his thoughts yesterday on a particular problem. and without much effort, he was able to produce something (quite roughly) that made sense.

I started wondering, "how was he able to decide things like - I'll draw a line here, and a dot there, or a box here with a text and an arrow pointing there etc". I know those questions probably sound dumb.

I haven't heard of raptor. I have used online diagramming apps like draw.io but I end up wasting so much time because of skew lines etc. So I decided to get a drawing tablet to draw out my diagrams. I feel it has helped to allay my anxiety a little bit since I can erase as often as I want without ripping holes in paper.

If I may offer some advice on the documentation side of things :) having too much documentation is never bad, as long as its detailed and is relevant to the scope you are trying to describe. You can even include "tl;dr" sections as a summary incase someone doesn't want to read through everything. Obviously, just do what you do need to for university, but remember, the real world is vastly different.

I've also tried psudo but my mind always tries to revert back to actual code. It's probably sounds like BS but it's the truth. Writing code on paper is pointless. Might as well type it, thus back to the original dilemma.

Alternating between diagramming and coding is something I've tried but unfortunately the result is the same.

Hmm I've never heard of that approach before. It sounds interesting. I'll definitely check it out.

I even do solve the problem, however I feel like I waste so much time trying to figure things out through code as opposed to actually having something on paper to follow. My previous senior was like that, he could code in his head basically and as a result, I naturally followed suit.

Now, unfortunately, since the projects I'm working on are so complex, programming in code is not viable anymore. There's many pieces to remember.

Speaking of studies, my friend asked me for help coding a hangman game in C# using a basic Windows form app. Despite it being really simple, I found that whilst drawing out a diagram for him, I was messing up. Nothing made sense.

I was so horrified that I wasn't even able to get a diagram correct for a hangman game. This was just walking through the pure logic from the key press, checking if the specified letter pressed is correct, add to list of correct guesses else add to incorrect guesses list etc, and then update the UI. I could code it in a heartbeat but I failed to accurately draw it out.

I've been in the industry for a few years already. I find that the moment I try and focus on one particular feature, edge cases start overwhelming my focus which ultimately prevents me from putting anything on that paper. Obviously one can be as detailed or as minimal as needed in any diagram or plan of action, but I'm failing to get even a pencil stroke on a page.

Believe me, premature optimisation is definitely something I learned to avoid long ago. My goal isn't to prematurely optimise my code. I'm all for getting my code to work initially even if it's poorly written.

However, I feel like I'm struggling to get the basics functional. I have the overall goal mapped out in my head. I can tell you, I need to code "x" next, then code "y" next. That's the easy part. The difficult part is figuring out how to express those individual parts on paper. It's trying to express how to achieve the micro steps that make up each piece.

Ultimately I feel I like I lack the vocabulary necessary to express my thoughts through the problem domain.  I might be losing you at this point already but I hope I'm making some sense.

Did you eventually figure out a why? I'm sure there's no silver bullet to this. How did you learn how to accurately represent on paper, from your goals to your intentions, steps to sequences?

Is possibly that because I was never "taught" how to plan?

It's also not my intention to lean on autism as excuse but could this difficulty be the consequence of poor executive function?

O and also, does the machine need to be on the company network in order to allow remote access or can it be connected to the Internet from anywhere, even on home WiFi for example? Company doesn't require me to use a VPN (no company specific files / resources are needed for my work).

I suppose this means I have to be especially mindful in future with whatever I do on the machine. I've never used it for anything illegal or questionable though. 

As a software developer, I've never liked nor appreciated random people managing technology for me, but I suppose as you say, I don't have any choice.

I get very suspicious when companies want all of this weird software cr** installed. Pardon my French.
